Something that is odorous has a noticeable smell — strong enough that you can detect it easily. The word simply means "having an odor" or "giving off a smell."
Is it a good smell or a bad smell?

This is where the word gets interesting. Technically, odorous can describe any strong smell — pleasant or unpleasant. But in modern everyday English, when people use the word "odorous," they usually mean a smell that is unpleasant or at least hard to ignore. Think garbage, wet clothes, a sweaty gym, or a blocked drain.

In older, literary, or poetic writing, however, you'll find odorous used for pleasant smells too — like fragrant flowers or spiced air. So the word is technically neutral at its core, but in practice today, it tends to lean toward the unpleasant side.

A simple way to remember this: if someone describes your cooking as "odorous," it's probably not a compliment.

Odorous implies that the smell is noticeable — not a faint whisper of a scent, but something your nose picks up clearly. You wouldn't usually call a very subtle, barely-there smell "odorous." The smell has to have some presence to it.

Odorous is not the kind of word you'd use in casual conversation. It belongs to formal writing, academic contexts, or literature. In everyday speech, people say "smelly," "stinky," "it reeks," or "it stinks" instead. If you read "odorous" in a newspaper, a novel, or a scientific text, that's right at home. Dropping it in a chat with friends would sound unusual or even funny.

• "The odorous dumpster outside the restaurant made it hard to walk past."
  • "After the rain, the sewage pipes left the street odorous all morning."
  • "Workers in the odorous chemical plant were required to wear protective masks."
  • (Literary usage, positive): "The garden was full of odorous roses blooming under the summer sun."
How is it different from similar words?

Understanding odorous becomes much clearer when you compare it to words that live nearby:

Fragrant — This specifically means a pleasant, sweet, or floral smell. A rose is fragrant. "Odorous" doesn't carry that guarantee of pleasantness — it's broader.

Malodorous — This means badly smelling — unpleasant, offensive. It's the negative version made explicit. "Malodorous" removes all ambiguity: it's definitely a bad smell. "Odorous" is more neutral in definition, even if it leans negative in practice.

Pungent — A sharp, strong, often biting smell. Think of raw onions, strong vinegar, or ammonia. Pungent highlights the sharpness and intensity of the smell. "Odorous" just says there's a noticeable smell without describing its character.

Aromatic — Usually a pleasant, rich, spicy, or distinctive smell. Coffee is aromatic. Spices are aromatic. This is clearly positive in tone. "Odorous" carries no such positive guarantee.

Odorless / Inodorous — The complete opposite of odorous. Something with no smell at all.

So think of it as a spectrum:

  • Fragrant / Aromatic → clearly nice smells
  • Odorous → noticeable smell (positive or, more commonly, unpleasant)
  • Pungent → sharp, strong, biting smell
  • Malodorous → clearly bad smell

• Odor (noun) — the smell itself. "There was a strange odor in the room."
  • Odorously (adverb) — in a way that produces a smell. "The factory vented its gases odorously into the air."
  • Odorousness (noun) — the quality of having a strong smell. "The odorousness of the fish market was overwhelming."

Odorous = having a strong, noticeable smell. It can technically go either way (pleasant or unpleasant), but in modern usage it almost always points to something that smells bad or at least overpowering. It's a formal, literary word — not casual speech. If you want to be specific about a good smell, say fragrant or aromatic. If you want to be specific about a bad smell, say malodorous. Odorous sits in the middle, usually nudging toward the unpleasant end.
